newsitem.title: CHINA: FUND VIEW - Peso float fails to surprise funds.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW - Peso float fails to surprise funds.

text.p: Friday's sharp depreciation of the Philippine peso against the U.S. dollar was "hardly unexpected", according to fund managers, but they questioned the sustainability of Manila's subsequent stock market rally.

Manila's evident lack of foreign exchange reserves in the face of speculative attack and last week's effective devaluation of the Thai baht made a break of the peso's band virtually inevitable, they said.

"One has to say the Philippines is not in as tricky position as Thailand, but when they're going for the investment buck out there, they are competing head on with Thailand. Now when you have a disparity in the two currencies, that doesn't help your cause," said James Wilson, institutional sales director at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. The Philippine peso plunged over 11 percent to 29.45 to the U.S. dollar after the central bank widened its trading band.
The move surprised some by spurring a roaring rally in the Manila stock exchange, with the main stock index soaring to close 7.57 percent higher at 2701.14 percent.
But fund managers in Hong Kong were divided in their interpretation, both of the peso flotation and its effect upon the stock market.

Some were picking up bargains but maintaining neutral weightings against the benchmark Morgan Stanley Capital International Asia ex-Japan index, while others were active sellers in anticipation of a worsening economic picture.
Despite the central bank's claim that a weaker currency could improve the nation's fiscal position, some fund managers questioned its effect both upon inflation and the trade deficit.
Funding a widening trade deficit in devalued pesos would hurt, as would increased inflationary pressure which would add to already-high levels of asset price inflation.

But improved export competitiveness and greater currency flexibility were welcomed, as was the removal of an investment disincentive against Thailand, where the stock market also rallied following the July 2 flotation of the baht.

"We've seen a rally in the stock market but that may not be sustainable.There are good things that come with devaluation and bad things. We'll have to see how it nets out," said David Descalzi, senior portfolio manager at Prudential Asia.
Descalzi said Prudential Asia halted order sales in the Philippines pending the outcome of the peso devaluation -- but others were buying into the rally.

"Looking at the depreciation and the way the stock market has moved, we can find some pretty good value in the market and we've moved to pick up stock with fundamental value," said one fund manager. "But we're staying neutral."

Many are also watching the fallout from Thailand's currency flotation. The initial reaction has been positive, but the nuts and bolts of Thailand's financial-sector restructuring have yet to take full effect.

Regardless, most institutional investors believe the economic impact of the devaluation in the Philippines is bound to be less painful than in Thailand. "I don't think the repercussions will be as severe as in Thailand. The Philippines is still at a more nascent stage of development in terms of its reliance on foreign capital," said Wilson.
